analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal money from going to earmarks hidden in committee reports and forces public disclosure of every earmark.
analysis.headline: The earmark disclosure bill, introduced with 22 cosponsors from both parties, never got a vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop federal agencies from spending money on "earmarks" — projects directed to a specific recipient — when those projects appear only in committee reports rather than in the actual law. It would also ban earmarks that were added behind closed doors by conference committees, unless they appeared in the version the House or Senate already passed. And it would require a public list of every earmark, with the sponsoring member named where possible, posted online for at least 72 hours before Congress votes on a bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would see every earmark and its sponsor posted online before a vote, and whose money could no longer be spent on projects that never appeared in the legislation itself. Ordinary members of Congress, who could no longer be outmaneuvered by hidden items slipped into reports.

how_it_helps.text: No federal agency could obligate funds for an earmark found only in a committee report or conference statement; the earmark would have to be written into the law itself [S3].
Agencies could not fund earmarks that were added in a conference committee but were never in the House-passed or Senate-passed version of the bill [S3].

Before the House considers a final bill or conference report, a list of all its earmarks, the member who proposed each one (when identifiable), and the governmental purpose of each would have to be posted on the Internet for at least 72 hours [S3].
The earmark definition covers grants, loans, loan guarantees, and contracts to private businesses, states, territories, and localities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress who direct earmarks to favored recipients, and the contractors, lobbying firms, and institutions that win those directed contracts and grants, who would lose the shield of hidden report language and back-room conference additions.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the appropriations process argue that report language and conference additions are long-standing tools Congress uses to direct federal spending toward local needs, and that requiring every earmark to appear in the bill text and survive a floor vote could push decisions toward executive agencies instead [S2].
The 72-hour public posting requirement would delay final consideration of spending bills, which could complicate passing appropriations on time at the end of a session [S3].
The rule change takes effect only at the start of the next Congress and applies only to Acts enacted after December 31, 2006, limiting its immediate effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency benefits are broad but hard to quantify: every earmark and its sponsor would be public before a vote, and money could not flow to projects that never passed either chamber. The costs are procedural — some delay in passing spending bills and a shift of some spending decisions away from Congress. For anyone who thinks directed spending should happen in the open, the benefits outweigh the frictions; the honest objection is that the bill curbs one of Congress's few direct tools for steering federal money to specific communities.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Flake introduced the bill on March 15, 2006, with 22 original cosponsors including members of both parties [S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Government Reform Committee and the Rules Committee for consideration of provisions in their jurisdictions [S5].
The full action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007, and the bill received no vote before then [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members who used hidden report language and conference additions to steer money to favored projects kept the status quo, along with the contractors and lobbyists who benefited from that process. Taxpayers got no disclosure requirement from this bill, though the House later adopted its own earmark disclosure rules under pressure from the same scandal-driven debate.

against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing or markup after referral

against.name: House Committee on Rules
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing or markup after referral; its jurisdiction covered the rule-change provisions of the bill

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 23 sponsors split roughly along the House's partisan makeup — 15 Republicans and 8 Democrats — and opposition came not from a recorded vote but from committee inaction.

industries.industry: Government contractors and other earmark recipients (private firms, states, universities, local projects)
industries.note: The bill would cut off funding for earmarks that appear only in committee reports or that were inserted in conference, and force public disclosure of every directed grant, loan guarantee, or contract. Recipients who rely on hidden report language would lose that channel.

Lobbyists earn fees for winning earmarks through report language and conference additions; the bill would require naming the sponsoring member and kill funding for items that never passed either chamber, reducing the value of that service.
